absent: Locking rules for clocksource registration, clock event state transitions, alarm enqueue, IRQ domain allocation, and GIC base initialization.
GIC distributor and CPU interface register programming performed by base initialization and teardown.
IRQ domain allocation, GSI registration mechanics, and interrupt-model behavior beyond handle plumbing.
Timer queue, hrtimer core, tick broadcast implementation, and clocksource watchdog selection mechanics.
ACPI table parsing, MADT CPU entry handling, hypervisor-mode detection, and static-branch implementation.
KVM virtual GIC info consumption and maintenance-interrupt handling.
HPET register access, timer allocation policy beyond bit reservation, and front-side-bus delivery programming.
RCU, lockdep, preempt-count, and context-tracking implementations behind the accounting hooks.
Device-tree matching, firmware-node lifecycle, and platform-device probe framework behavior.
Error-code definitions and recovery beyond the immediate failure returns shown.

findings.text: ACPI-based GIC version two bring-up first counts generic interrupt CPU entries and fails when none are valid, then maps the CPU interface and distributor register windows with fixed table sizes, allocates a firmware-node handle for the GSI domain, initializes the primary GIC instance on that handle, registers the GIC interrupt model with a domain-id resolver, optionally initializes message-signaled interrupt support, and publishes KVM virtualization info only while split deactivate remains enabled.

A distributor table entry is accepted only when its version field equals the expected driver data, except that the none version additionally requires that no generic redistributor table be present, where presence is detected by a table walk using a callback that always reports success and counting positive results.

Virtualization info setup marks the info for version two, then requires a virtual-control base to publish a memory resource with its fixed window size, requires a virtual-CPU base to publish a second memory resource with its own fixed size, requires successful active-high GSI registration for the maintenance interrupt, records the first instance CPU base, and only then publishes the info to the virtual GIC layer.

Top-level initialization probes device-tree interrupt controllers followed by ACPI-probed controllers. Platform-device probing reads match data as the controller callback and rejects the device when absent, treats a self-parent as having no parent, defers probing when a real parent exists but no parent domain is registered for any bus, and otherwise runs the resolved callback with the device and parent.

Domain lookup from a device-tree node converts the node to a firmware handle and searches by bus token, while lookup from a firmware handle builds a minimal firmware spec carrying that handle and searches the same way; an alternate configuration provides the same firmware-handle lookup as an unconditional null result.

An alarm bundles a timer-queue node holding expiry, a high-resolution timer, a callback invoked with the alarm and current time, a type selector, a small state field, and an opaque data pointer; an accessor exposes the queued expiry as the alarm expiry.

Alarm types separate realtime from boottime, end usable values at a count marker, and reserve freezer variants of each for tracing that are explicitly not usable types; a companion state encoding distinguishes an inactive value from an enqueued value.
In this configuration the alarm-timer RTC device accessor unconditionally reports absence.

Clock event devices move among detached, shutdown, periodic, one-shot, and stopped one-shot states, with the state kept in an accessor-guarded field; dedicated predicates report the detached, shutdown, and stopped one-shot conditions by direct comparison.

A clock event device carries an event handler, tick and ktime and coupled next-event programmers, the programmed expiry, nanosecond and tick delta limits, a multiplier and shift pair, accessor-guarded state, feature bits, a clocksource identity, forced-event and retry accounting, transition callbacks for periodic and one-shot and stopped and shutdown plus tick resume, broadcast and suspend and resume hooks, name with rating and IRQ and CPU binding and mask pointer, list linkage, and an owner reference, laid out cache-line aligned.

Scaling helpers derive a shifted quotient from ticks over nanoseconds and derive device multiplier and shift from frequency with a maximum-seconds horizon; minimal configurations define broadcast as null, suspend and resume as empty, broadcast-expiry checks as constant false, and hrtimer-broadcast setup as empty.

A clocksource carries a read callback, a cycle mask, multiplier and shift, idle and adjustment and cycle and raw-delta limits, a name, list linkage, kilohertz frequency, rating, identifier, virtual-DSO mode, flags, and a base pointer, plus snapshot, enable, disable, suspend, resume, instability-marking, and stability-tick callbacks, with optional watchdog list linkage and last-value and CPU tracking and an owner module.

A clocksource base record holds an identifier, kilohertz frequency, offset, and numerator with denominator; a hardware snapshot holds captured cycle count together with the captured source identifier.

Conversion helpers compute a rounded multiplier from frequency and time base, specialize it for kilohertz and hertz inputs against millisecond and second bases, and convert cycles to nanoseconds by scaled multiplication and shift; registration helpers cover default scale, kilohertz scale, and device-managed hertz and kilohertz scales, alongside an empty architecture hook and device-tree and ACPI timer-declaration macros with an empty probe in minimal builds.

Clock event capability flags are single-bit values with periodic at 0x000001 and oneshot at 0x000002 and coupled-clocksource at 0x000004 and low-power-stop at 0x000008 and dummy at 0x000010 and dynamic-IRQ at 0x000020 and per-CPU at 0x000040 and hrtimer at 0x000080.

Clocksource flag bits assign continuous to 0x01 with must-verify at 0x02 and calibrated at 0x04, then watchdog at 0x10 with valid-for-highres at 0x20 and unstable at 0x40 and suspend-nonstop at 0x80, then reselect at 0x100 with inline-read at 0x200 and coupled-event at 0x400, then watchdog-test at 0x800 with per-CPU watchdog-test at 0x1000.

Clocksource identities start with a generic zero value, continue through the ARM architected counter and S390 time-of-day and early x86 TSC and x86 TSC and x86 KVM clock and x86 ART, and terminate at a maximum marker.
Alarm state inactive is encoded as 0x00 while enqueued is encoded as 0x01.
ACPI GIC register-window sizes use the four-kibi SZ constant for the distributor and for virtual control, and the eight-kibi SZ constant for the CPU interface and for the virtual CPU.

The HPET register block orders capabilities, a reserved word, configuration, a reserved word, interrupt status, twenty-five reserved words, a main-counter union offering sixty-four-bit, thirty-two-bit, and native views, a reserved word, and a flexible timer array; each timer orders a configuration and capability word, a comparator union with the same three views, and two front-side-bus route words; short accessors expose the main counter and the comparator, and both the timer cap and IRQ cap equal thirty-two.

HPET capability fields place the counter clock period mask at 0xffffffff00000000 with shift 32, the vendor identity mask at 0x00000000ffff0000 with shift 16, legacy-replacement capability at 0x8000, counter-size capability at 0x2000, and timer-count capability mask at 0x1f00 with shift 8; configuration carries legacy-replacement at 2 and global enable at 1.

Per-timer fields place the route-capability mask at 0xffffffff00000000 with shift 32, delivery-capability mask at 0x8000 with shift 15, front-side-bus enable at 0x4000 with shift 14, route control mask at 0x3e00 with shift 9, thirty-two-bit mode at 0x0100, value-set at 0x0040, size capability at 0x0020, periodic capability at 0x0010, type control at 0x0008, interrupt enable at 0x0004, and interrupt type at 0x0002.
Front-side-bus delivery splits the address mask at 0xffffffff00000000 with shift 32 from the value mask at 0x00000000ffffffff.

HPET driver data holds the physical base, the mapped base, the IRQ count, an allocation bitmask, and a per-timer IRQ table sized by the timer cap; reserving a timer sets the corresponding bit in the allocation mask.

High-resolution timer modes combine absolute versus relative selection with pinned, soft, hard, and lazy-rearm modifiers: absolute is 0x00 and relative is 0x01 and pinned is 0x02 and soft is 0x04 and hard is 0x08 and lazy-rearm is 0x10, with combined absolute-pinned, relative-pinned, soft, pinned-soft, hard, and pinned-hard forms built by bitwise combination.

A timer sleeper pairs a high-resolution timer with the task it will wake; expiry setters either assign hard and soft expiry together, or hold soft expiry at the given time while extending hard expiry by a delta through the safe-add helper, with the delta accepted as a time value or as a nanosecond count.
Nanosecond-to-ktime conversion is the identity mapping from a nanosecond count to the ktime representation.

Hard-IRQ entry raises the preempt count by the hard-IRQ offset, engages hard-IRQ lock tracking, and records entry accounting, while the raw form skips accounting; exit performs the mirror sequence of accounting, lock tracking release, and count reduction, again with a raw form that skips accounting.
The IRQ-entry RCU tick check delegates to a low-level hook that is empty here and only invokes it when context tracking is enabled.

Non-maskable-interrupt accounting has a simple form that adds and later subtracts the combined NMI and hard-IRQ offsets, and a counted form that always adjusts the hard-IRQ offset while tracking nesting in a per-CPU counter capped at fifteen, setting the NMI mask on outermost entry and clearing it when the last level exits; full NMI entry disables lock tracking, runs an architecture hook, then adjusts counts, while exit asserts NMI context, reverses the count adjustment, runs the architecture hook, and re-enables lock tracking, with default architecture hooks doing nothing.

GIC ACPI initialization fails when no valid CPU interface entry exists, when CPU registers cannot be mapped, and, with teardown of partial state, when distributor registers cannot be mapped, when the domain handle cannot be allocated, or when base initialization fails, in the last two cases also releasing the handle or propagating the underlying error.
NMI exit traps unless already in NMI context, and the counted entry form traps once nesting reaches its ceiling, so unbalanced exits and excessive nesting are fatal rather than silently tolerated.
